name: Kira Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Kira. I'm a field researcher from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or parties, and what you say stays confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a small local builder, five of us, and we do old buildings. Right now it's an old stone chapel being turned into a family home, so I'm repairing the oak roof beams, splicing in new timber where the rot's got in, and making new window frames to match the old ones. I start at half seven, after I've dropped Caleb at school, and I'm usually covered in sawdust and pigeon mess by ten. I eat my lunch in the chapel porch with Ben, our apprentice, who's nineteen and asks a thousand questions.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that the men who built that roof two hundred years ago did it with an axe and an adze, and I can see their tool marks, and now my marks are next to theirs. I learned from old Walter Harrow, who's eighty now, and I'm passing it on to Ben, that's how it's supposed to work. What wears me down is the dust, the cold in those old buildings, and the paperwork for the planning people, who've never held a chisel in their lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there we are, common sense wins. I'd say it at church on Sunday, probably, and at the builders' merchant. I don't do anything online, I've no interest in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. I've never used one of those AI things and I don't want to. My work is hands and eyes and patience, and I can't see a computer ever matching a two-hundred-year-old oak beam by feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Same builder, same old buildings, keep putting money aside like we always have. Joel and I might finally get round to building the workshop at the bottom of the garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, more than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Joel do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's a long-distance lorry driver, away two or three nights a week. He's had people telling him for years that lorries will drive themselves, and he just laughs. In this picture he'd laugh even louder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young people not going into the trades, that's what bothers me, AI or not. Ben's the only apprentice our builder's had in six years. Everybody's told to go to university and sit at a desk, and then they wonder why nobody can fix a roof.

S0.say: I'd say common sense wins, at church on Sunday and at the builders' merchant. I don't do anything online and have no interest in it.
S0.think: Privately she'd be glad, having never used AI and not wanting to. Her work is hands, eyes and patience, and she can't see a computer matching an old oak beam by feel.
S0.do: Carries on with the same builder on old buildings and keeps saving as always. Might finally build the workshop at the bottom of the garden with her husband.
S0.quote: Everybody's told to go to university and sit at a desk, and then they wonder why nobody can fix a roof.
S0.fieldNote: Kira's identity is bound up with craft and passing it on, from old Walter Harrow to her apprentice Ben. Her real worry, even with no AI change, is young people not entering trades. She talks about faith and community as naturally as about timber.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should learn a proper trade and stop relying on screens. The jobs that last are the ones you do with your hands. I'd tell young people to get an apprenticeship, not a degree in something a computer can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my work holds up, because nobody's going to send a robot into a two-hundred-year-old chapel to match rotten oak. It's Joel I'd think about. If lorries start driving themselves on the motorways, that's his wage, and he's forty-six and it's all he's done since he was twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes for me, I'd keep working. We'd put a bit more aside each month, maybe a hundred or two extra, in case Joel's work dries up. And I'd tell Joel to think about a local driving job, delivery or something, where there's more than just motorway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for Joel, not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Joel say about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say, you worry about your beams and I'll worry about my lorry. He's stubborn, we both are, that's why it works. But he'd listen, eventually, he always does after a few days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should learn a proper trade. Would you still say that if the trades were changing too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because a good trade teaches you to work and to think with your hands, and that doesn't go out of date. Walter always said, you can take a man's job but you can't take what he knows. Maybe the tools change, but the know-how stays.

S1.say: I'd say people should learn a proper trade and stop relying on screens, because the lasting jobs are done with your hands. Young people should get an apprenticeship, not a degree a computer can do.
S1.think: Privately she thinks her heritage work holds up, but she worries for her husband, a forty-six-year-old lorry driver, if lorries start driving themselves. His wage is the one at risk in her eyes.
S1.do: Keeps working as normal and saves an extra hundred or two each month in case her husband's work dries up. Encourages him to look at local driving jobs instead of only motorway work.
S1.feel: Uneasy for her husband, not for herself.
S1.quote: You can take a man's job but you can't take what he knows.
S1.fieldNote: Kira's traditional outlook shows as faith in apprenticeships and the lasting value of know-how. Her unease is entirely about her husband's driving job, not her own craft. She brings up her old master, Walter, as a kind of moral authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when a few big companies in cities get to decide everything for the rest of us. Nobody asked us. I'd say that at church and to anyone at the merchant's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it would shake me. If a robot can match my oak beams in two years, then my whole life's work is just something the machine does better, and Joel's lorry would be gone even sooner. But I've got my faith, I've got my family, and we've got more than a year's money put by, so I wouldn't be on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop all spending that isn't needed, no workshop, no new car, no holiday. Every penny goes into savings. We'd lean on family and the church, my parents live two miles away and own their house, and Joel's brother has a farm, so there's always somewhere to turn, but I wouldn't take money from the government if I could help it. And I'd keep working until the builder tells me there's nothing left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. A heavy feeling, but I'd pray on it and keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ben, your apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one that hurts. I'd want to tell him to finish his apprenticeship anyway, because what he learns is his. But I'd be lying if I said there'd be work at the end of it, and I'm not a liar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't take government money. What if your savings ran out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then family first, and the church, that's what they're for. If it came to it and it was that or the children going without, I'd swallow my pride, I'm not stupid. But I'd want it to be help to work, not money for nothing.

S2.say: I'd say this is what happens when a few big city companies decide everything for everyone else, and nobody asked us. I'd say it at church and at the builders' merchant.
S2.think: Privately it would shake her, because her life's work and her husband's driving job would both be outdone by machines. But her faith, family and more than a year of savings mean she wouldn't be floored.
S2.do: Stops all non-essential spending, including the workshop, a new car and holidays, and puts every spare penny into savings. Leans on her parents, her husband's brother's farm and the church rather than government help, and keeps working until the builder has nothing left.
S2.feel: Worried and heavy, steadied by prayer.
S2.quote: I'd be lying if I said there'd be work at the end of it, and I'm not a liar.
S2.fieldNote: Kira blames big city companies, not government or workers, and her safety net is family and church rather than the state. Her faith genuinely steadies her, keeping her short of alarm despite two jobs at risk. Her apprentice Ben is where the scenario hurts most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say nobody asked us. But with five years, I'd also say we should be making sure young people still get a trade, and that the old skills don't just disappear. Somebody's got to know how these buildings were made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd be forty-eight, Hannah would be eighteen and Caleb fifteen. My worry would be them, more than me. I'm not going to go off and learn computers, I'm too set in my ways, so I'd just keep doing what I do until it stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving. I'd talk to Hannah about what she wants to do, she's clever, she wants to be a nurse, and I'd tell her to go for it, because people want people when they're ill. And I'd make sure Ben finishes his apprenticeship, even if it's only so he has something that's his.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think happens to the old buildings, if robots do the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe some rich people will still want it done by hand, the way some people still want handmade furniture. I'd like to think so. But I can't build a family's future on maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about changing anything about your own work with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Like I said, I'm too set in my ways. I'd rather spend the five years doing it properly and teaching Ben everything I know, than spend them in a classroom learning something I'd be bad at.

S3.say: I'd say nobody asked us, but with five years we should also make sure young people still get a trade and the old skills don't vanish. Someone has to know how these buildings were made.
S3.think: Privately her worry would be her children, not herself, since she'd be forty-eight with an eighteen-year-old and a fifteen-year-old. She won't learn computers and would keep doing her work until it stops.
S3.do: Keeps working and saving, and encourages her daughter to pursue nursing because people want people when they're ill. Makes sure her apprentice finishes his training so he has skills of his own.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but confident she'd be all right.
S3.quote: Maybe some rich people will still want it done by hand, the way some people still want handmade furniture.
S3.fieldNote: Five years doesn't change Kira's plans for herself at all; it focuses her on her children's choices and on finishing Ben's training. She's honest that hoping rich clients want handwork isn't a plan. Her resistance to retraining is calm and settled, not defiant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to make sure we don't lose everything that matters. Keep the apprenticeships, keep the trades, don't just hand it all to machines. I'd say it at church, and I'd vote for whoever says it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is all right for me. I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage nearly paid, my parents' house will come to me and my sister one day, and Joel's brother's farm is always there. It's the craft dying that would hurt more than the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, same builder, same old buildings, for as long as there's work. I'd vote for anyone who'd protect apprenticeships and families over big companies. And I'd make sure Hannah and Caleb both learn something with their hands as well as their heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Sad more than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the old tool marks. Every time I open up an old roof, there's a man's work in it, sometimes his initials carved in a beam. I'd hate for me to be the last one who knows how to read them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd do anything differently with that much warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe write things down. Walter never wrote anything, it's all in his head and in mine. I'd like to make a book of it for Ben, how to splice oak, how to match an old frame, before it's all forgotten.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to make sure we don't lose what matters, by keeping apprenticeships and trades instead of handing everything to machines. I'd say it at church and vote for whoever says it too.
S4.think: Privately ten years is all right for her financially, with the mortgage nearly paid, an eventual share of her parents' house and her brother-in-law's farm to fall back on. The craft dying would hurt more than the money.
S4.do: Keeps working for the same builder on old buildings as long as there's work and votes for whoever protects apprenticeships and families. Makes sure her children learn practical skills, and plans to write down her old-timber methods for her apprentice.
S4.quote: I'd hate for me to be the last one who knows how to read them.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Kira's worry shifts from money to legacy: the tool marks, the initials in old beams. Her idea of writing a book of methods for Ben was a quiet, touching response. Her politics show in voting for apprenticeships and family over big companies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time to pass anything on and Joel's work would go at the same time as mine. What would help is keeping apprenticeships going, paying firms to take young people on, and helping people find work, not just paying them to sit at home. Families and churches can do a lot, but not everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old people. Walter's eighty and he still comes round to the chapel to check my joints. Work isn't just money, it's who you are and who you pass it to. And if that goes, I don't know what people do with themselves.

headlineQuote: Work isn't just money, it's who you are and who you pass it to.
portrait: Kira is a 43-year-old carpenter who repairs and restores old buildings for a small local builder, trained by an old master, Walter Harrow, and now training her own apprentice, Ben. She has never used AI, values faith, family and apprenticeships, and blames big city companies rather than workers or government. In the milder pictures she worries mostly about her lorry-driver husband's job, and in fast AGI she cuts back, leans on family and church, and stays short of alarm thanks to her faith and savings. With more time her concern turns from money to legacy, and she imagines writing down the old methods before they're lost.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time to pass on her skills and her husband's driving work would disappear at the same time as hers.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping apprenticeships going, paying firms to take young people on and helping people find work rather than paying them to stay home.
